title: Runtime surface guidelines: kernels, scheduler, and KV-cache integration
abstract: Practical guidance for the runtime API surface that reconciles kernel selection signals, scheduler priorities, and KV cache semantics. Focused on request schema fields, error taxonomy, and compatibility guarantees that keep hosted/dedicated/private deployments interoperable.
content:
Purpose and scope
This note captures a pragmatic, implementation-minded API surface for the serving runtime where three subsystems meet: kernel selection, request scheduling, and the KV-cache layer. It is written for engineers implementing the runtime and SDKs, and for platform/config tooling that must reason about backward/forward compatibility. The goal is to provide clear, minimal primitives in the request/response envelope that allow coordination across the three subsystems without exposing internal runtime complexity to end users.

Principles and constraints
- Minimal visible surface: Keep request fields small and stable; avoid leaking internal kernel names or hardware topology into customer-facing APIs.
- Backward-compatible extension: Additive fields only; unknown fields must be ignored by older servers and clients.
- Deterministic fallback behavior: Define explicit semantics for when kernels, scheduling tiers, or caches are unavailable.
- Observable decisions: Include optional tracing fields so decisions can be reconstructed in logs and traces.

High-level envelope (informal)
- request_id: string (client-provided optional; server will return canonical id)
- model: string (logical model name; not runtime binary)
- model_variant: optional string (semantic hint for smaller/quantized variant)
- sequence_len_hint: optional int (expected tokens to generate; helps kernel/queue sizing)
- priority: optional string (low | normal | high | realtime)
- cache_policy: optional string (default | prefer-cache | bypass-cache)
- kernel_hints: optional list of strings (non-binding hints, e.g. "low-memory", "int8-friendly")
- trace_tags: optional map (opaque key/value for traces; must be ignored unless explicitly whitelisted)

Notes on each field
- request_id: If provided, used for idempotency and KV-cache lookup keys. The runtime must still synthesize a server_request_id and return it. Clients should prefer stable ids for retries.
- model/model_variant: Logical identifiers; the runtime maps these to concrete artifacts. Model_variant can be used for compatibility-aware downgrade (e.g., "gptx-lite-q4"). Mapping rules live in the model catalog and are out-of-band to the request.
- sequence_len_hint: Not a hard limit. Scheduler and kernel selection can use this for buffer allocation and to choose attention kernels optimized for short or long contexts.
- priority: Scheduler uses this as a soft lane. Realtime requests bypass batching heuristics where feasible; high is placed ahead of normal but does not preempt in-progress token generation.
- cache_policy: Controls prefix/KV cache usage. prefer-cache may increase latency variance due to cache-loading paths; bypass-cache forces fresh generation and should be honored immediately.
- kernel_hints: Hints only; they do not change correctness. Kernel selection is an internal decision. Hints enable richer routing in private/dedicated deployments where customers trust the operator.

Compatibility guarantees and versioning rules
- Additive fields: Servers must ignore unknown top-level fields. Clients must be robust to missing fields (assume defaults).
- Response stability: Fields present in a response in vN should not be removed in vN+1 without a deprecation window. Removing optional trace fields is permitted if documented.
- Model compatibility: The runtime guarantees that a logical model name maps to some artifact that preserves the documented input/output contract (tokenization, special tokens). Breaking changes require a new logical name.
- Kernel-opaque responses: The runtime must never expose kernel internal identifiers as part of standard responses. If kernel telemetry is emitted, it must be under an opt-in internal telemetry channel.

Error taxonomy and surface
Design goals: errors must be actionable, stable, and machine-friendly. Each error has: code (stable short string), http_status, retryability (yes/no/conditional), and human_message. We return both code and message fields.

Suggested common codes (non-exhaustive)
- model_not_found (404) -> retryable: no; message: "Requested model/version not available"
- model_compatibility_error (400) -> retryable: no; message: "Input incompatible with model tokenization/schema"
- kernel_unavailable (503) -> retryable: conditional; message: "Requested execution kernel currently unavailable; can retry or route to fallback"
- scheduling_throttled (429) -> retryable: yes (backoff required); message: "Request throttled by scheduler; use retry-after"
- cache_miss_fetch_error (502) -> retryable: yes; message: "KV cache backend returned error while loading prefix"
- deterministic_timeout (504) -> retryable: conditional; message: "Request exceeded runtime timeout budget"
- internal_execution_error (500) -> retryable: no by default; message: "Unexpected runtime error; collect logs and contact support"

Conditional retry guidance
- kernel_unavailable: automatic routing/fallback may be possible in-hosted mode; dedicated/private contracts may surface additional fallback semantics in the deploy config.
- deterministic_timeout: client may retry with smaller sequence_len_hint or lower temperature; otherwise escalate.

Scheduler semantics and lanes
- Lanes: realtime (lowest batching, tight latency SLO), high (priority ordering, moderate batching), normal (default), low (best-effort batching).
- Within a lane: FIFO with batching-aware grouping. Exact ordering across lanes: realtime > high > normal > low.
- Preemption: No preemption of already-started generation. Scheduling decisions apply at request admission time.
- Batching policy: Scheduler may aggregate compatible requests into a batch if model and model_variant are compatible and cache_policy != bypass-cache. Compatibility is primarily determined by tokenization/schema and whether requests require deterministic KV cache state.

Integrating kernel selection with scheduler
- Kernel selection inputs: model, model_variant, sequence_len_hint, kernel_hints, trace_tags, hardware capabilities (internal).
- Kernel selection outputs (internal): preferred kernel id, quantization mode, attention kernel variant, memory reservation. These are not exposed to the client, but the runtime should populate trace fields for observability when requested.
- Scheduling constraints: If kernel selection indicates a specialized kernel (e.g., float16-block-attn), scheduler should treat the request as only batchable with other requests that map to the same kernel family to avoid costly kernel-switch overheads mid-batch.

KV-cache semantics and consistency model
- Prefix KV cache is best-effort and eventually consistent in distributed deployments. The runtime exposes these guarantees to avoid accidental reliance on strong consistency.
- Cache key derivation: By default: cache_key = hash(model, model_variant, canonicalized_prompt, request_id?). The default should be stable and documented. If request_id is present, allow optional inclusion to support deterministic reuse across retries; default excludes request_id to maximize hit rate across equivalent prompts.
- Invalidation: No automatic cross-request invalidation is guaranteed. Clients that need strict single-writer semantics should include a per-session scope in the canonicalized_prompt or use a session-scoped key provided by the runtime.
- Cache_policy semantics:
  - default: use cache if available; otherwise generate and populate cache.
  - prefer-cache: if cache miss, attempt to fetch asynchronous cache warm (may increase latency) or consult fallback variant.
  - bypass-cache: do not read or populate prefix cache; still may use ephemeral KV for beam/internal generation but must not write persistent cache entries.

KV-cache and compatibility tradeoffs
- Because cache keys encode model and tokenization assumptions, model upgrades that change tokenization must either change logical model names or invalidate existing caches (operator action). The API will emit a model_catalog_version in admin telemetry so clients and operators can correlate cache hit-rate shifts.
- Runtime must tolerate cache entries produced by older model artifacts but should fall back gracefully if decoding of cached states fails; return a cache_miss_fetch_error or proceed with fresh generation depending on cache_policy.

Trace and observability fields (opt-in)
- telemetry.request_path: small list of stage tags (admission -> kernel_select -> batch -> execute -> finalize)
- telemetry.kernel_family: opaque string for internal grouping (only when allowed)
- telemetry.scheduler_lane: the lane chosen
- telemetry.cache_decision: hit | miss | bypass | error
- Privacy: trace_tags must be opt-in; by default traces exclude user-visible prompt text.

SDK and client guidance
- Retry semantics: Respect retry-after for 429. Use exponential backoff for conditional retryable errors. On deterministic_timeout consider lowering sequence_len_hint or splitting requests.
- Idempotency: Provide request_id for safe retries; the runtime will use it to deduplicate KV-cache writes in many configurations. Do not rely on request_id across model changes.
- Kernel hints: Use sparingly. These hints are for advanced customers in dedicated/private deployments. They should never be required for correctness.

Operational notes for deploys (private/dedicated)
- Local kernel families: Operators can expose additional kernel_hints accepted by the runtime. Those hints must be documented in the deployment manifest and treated as non-portable.
- Cache eviction policies: Document and surface eviction windows per model in the console. Operators should plan cache invalidation when rolling tokenizers or major model changes.
- Fallback policies: Provide a deployment-level policy for kernel_unavailable and scheduling_throttled that documents whether requests will be routed to a fallback model_variant or fail fast.

Open questions and action items
- Formalize cache key canonicalization: produce a deterministic spec (ticket: JIRA-ENG-782).
- Define telemetry opt-in API contract across hosted and private deployments (GH-PR-2103).
- Decide whether request_id should be included in cache_key by default for session-oriented applications.

Appendix: example envelopes
Client request (JSON):
{
  "request_id": "client:1234",
  "model": "redwood-alpha-7b",
  "model_variant": "alpha-7b-q4",
  "sequence_len_hint": 256,
  "priority": "high",
  "cache_policy": "prefer-cache",
  "kernel_hints": ["int8-friendly"],
  "trace_tags": {"test-run": "canary-3"},
  "input": "Write a short haiku about runtime caches."
}

Successful response (JSON):
{
  "server_request_id": "srv:abcd-ef01",
  "request_id": "client:1234",
  "status": "ok",
  "generated_text": "...haiku...",
  "telemetry": {"scheduler_lane": "high", "cache_decision": "hit"},
  "model": "redwood-alpha-7b",
  "model_variant": "alpha-7b-q4"
}

Error response (JSON):
{
  "server_request_id": "srv:abcd-ef02",
  "request_id": "client:1235",
  "status": "error",
  "error": {"code": "kernel_unavailable", "http_status": 503, "message": "Requested execution kernel currently unavailable; try retrying or use fallback variant."}
}

Closing note
This is a working doc. It favors concrete, implementable rules that preserve portability between hosted/dedicated/private deployments while exposing enough surface to reason about performance and correctness tradeoffs. The next revision should consolidate canonical cache-key rules and a minimal schema for the telemetry opt-in API.
